newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan president ends "corrupt" Bhutto rule.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan president ends "corrupt" Bhutto rule.

text.p: Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto was sacked on Tuesday for a second time in her turbulent political career by the country's president, who accused her beleaguered government of corruption, nepotism and misrule.
President Farooq Leghari accused Bhutto's government of fostering corruption, undermining the judiciary and failing to stop extra-judicial killings in Karachi and elsewhere.

"Public faith in the integrity and honesty of the government has disappeared," he said in a blistering indictment of her three-year rule. Corruption and nepotism had made it impossible for the government to function, he said in a proclamation.
Leghari later swore in veteran politician Meraj Khalid, 80, at the head of a nine-member caretaker cabinet to supervise early elections the president called for February 3, 1997.
"Our first priority will be to hold free, fair and impartial elections," Khalid told reporters at his home earlier.
State television showed a recording of the oath-taking ceremony and said it would carry a live broadcast to the nation by Leghari later in the day, but gave no time.
Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) denounced what it called "the unconstitutional dismissal of the elected government in the darkness of night".
But main opposition leader Nawaz Sharif said Bhutto's fall was "deliverance for the people" and expressed confidence his Pakistan Muslim League would win the general elections.
Witnesses said soldiers in the Punjab provincial capital of Lahore had detained Bhutto's husband, Asif Ali Zardari, who has been at the centre of corruption allegations.

The military, which has ruled the Islamic nation for 24 years of the nearly 50 years of independence since 1947, kept a low profile, but political observers said Leghari could not have acted without securing approval and cooperation of the generals.

Troops moved into the capital Islamabad in the early hours to guard key installations, but stayed off the streets, which remained calm, apart from a few firecrackers let off by celebrating shopkeepers. Schools and businesses opened as usual.
In nearby Rawalpindi, about 200 opposition party supporters fired assault rifles into the air to celebrate Bhutto's ouster and hoisted a traffic policeman on to their shoulders in joy.
Neighbouring India reacted calmly to the news, saying it was an internal affair that would not affect ties with Pakistan, with whom Delhi has fought three wars since the end of British rule in 1947.
"We see these events as Pakistan's internal developments and are following them closely," Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said in Zimbabwe, where he was attending a trade summit meeting.
Bhutto was holed up at the official prime minister's residence, with her telephone lines out of action and troops turning back former ministers who tried to visit her.

But the PPP chief minister of North West Frontier Province, Aftab Sherpao, was allowed in to see her in the afternoon after visiting Leghari. "What has happened has been a big shock for her," Sherpao told reporters before entering Bhutto's residence.
"We have been fighting against it and now it has happened," he said of her dismissal. Sherpao said Bhutto, 43, was unlikely to take the removal of her three-year-old government meekly.
"She is a fighter," he said.

Bhutto's government had been beset by mounting political and economic crises, including the killing of her brother and persistent allegations of corruption, but she had sworn to keep going until scheduled elections in October 1998.
Imran Khan, Pakistan's cricketer-turned-politician, welcomed Bhutto's sacking, but said his party would only fight the polls if electoral reforms and a national census were implemented.
Imran, who founded the Tehreek-e-Insaaf (Justice Movement) party this year, told Reuters Television his party contributed to Bhutto's fall by focussing attention on corruption.
The leader of the religious Jamaat-i-Islamic opposition party also hailed Bhutto's dismissal, but said corrupt politicians should be brought to book before any new elections.
"We want the caretaker government to start a process of accountability to be conducted by the supreme judiciary of the country," Qazi Hussain Ahmed told a news conference.

Jamaat-i-Islami brought several thousand supporters on to the streets of Islamabad and nearby Rawalpindi last week for anti-corruption protests that provoked a security clampdown and half-paralysed the two cities for three days.
An International Monetary Fund official said a visiting IMF mission would pursue talks with the caretaker government on reactivation of a $600 million standby loan.
Visiting British Shadow Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said serious problems, including economic chaos, rows over the judiciary and corruption, had marred Bhutto's administration.
"Obviously, the interest of the international community is that the election commitment be honoured...,"he said.
Bhutto had been in power since general elections in October 1993. Her first term lasted 20 months before then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan sacked her in 1990 for similar reasons.
The president has constitutional powers to dismiss elected governments and dissolve parliament's lower house.
